tour.title: Yanaka & Ueno: Lanes of the Old Low City
tour.summary: Ueno's battlefield park, a postwar black-market street, then the old low city that the fires missed — a shopping lane, a sunset staircase, a 1706 shrine and a cemetery of famous dead.
tour.overviewText:
Tokyo is a city of wood that burned and concrete that replaced it. What you land in — glass towers, elevated expressways, a subway map like a circuit board — was built over twice: after the earthquake and firestorms of 1923, and again after the firebombing of 1945. This walk goes to the part the fires missed: Ueno, Yanaka and Nezu kept their old street pattern, small wooden houses and temple lanes.

In Tokyo, geography is social history. Edo — the city's name until 1868 — was a castle town laid out by class. The shōgun, the military ruler who governed while the emperor reigned as a figurehead in Kyoto, lived on the breezy western hills with his samurai: the yamanote, the high city. Merchants and artisans were packed into the flat, drained marshland east of the castle: the shitamachi, the low city, where the workshops, wharves and markets were. The names still carry meaning: shitamachi suggests small shops, loud streets and old families; yamanote suggests money and manners. You are walking in the shitamachi: confusingly, on high ground, because part of the old low city sat on this bluff.

Two things made that bluff a survivor. The first is fire. Edo was built of paper, wood and pine resin and burned constantly; one blaze in 1657 is estimated to have killed around a hundred thousand people. So the shōguns pushed big temples outward and kept open ground as firebreaks — which is why Yanaka is dense with temple land, and why a temple graveyard here could become the city's largest public cemetery. The second is the accident of 1868 and 1945: the civil war that ended the shogunate burned Ueno's great temple but died out on this plateau, and the firebombing of March 1945 left Yanaka comparatively intact while the flatlands went. What remains is not a preserved village but a working neighbourhood that happens to keep its old bones.

The walk lasts about half a day and runs a little under seven kilometres. It starts in Ueno Park, above Shinobazu Pond, where a surviving 1631 temple hall stands among the museums and where the last battle of the shogunate was fought; drops east into the noise of Ameyoko, the postwar black market; then climbs north into Yanaka's shopping lane, the sunset steps, a three-century-old shrine, the great cemetery, and finally Sendagi, where the city goes quiet. Mostly flat, with two short climbs and a lot of standing still.

February in Tokyo is cold, dry and often brilliantly clear — around 3 to 11 degrees, sunset soon after five — which is why the walk is best begun in early afternoon: the steps deserve the sun, and nearly every shop shuts by six. Almost everything is free; the likely costs are a shrine garden in spring and whatever you eat. Bring small change and an IC transit card for the trains. One calendar note: Japan does not celebrate the lunar New Year, so if your visit lands on Chinese New Year the city will be in its ordinary February — the local festival is Setsubun, on 3 February, when shrines and temples throw beans to drive out the year's bad luck.

Wear shoes you can walk in, and go slowly. The old city rewards people who stop.
tour.difficulty: Easy, with two short climbs. Flat pavements and lanes for most of the route, but the bluffs at Ueno and Nippori involve steps and slopes, and the last stretch through the cemetery is a gravel and stone avenue. Yanaka Ginza is three metres wide and gets crowded at weekends. Distances feel longer than they are because of the stopping.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 12:30 to 1pm. Museums and temples are open, Yanaka Ginza is trading, and you reach the Sunset Steps and the cemetery in the last hour of light — in February the sun is down soon after 5pm. Mornings work, but you would hit Yanaka Ginza before it wakes and the steps with the sun still high. Avoid saving the shopping street for the evening; most shops close by 6pm.

stops.name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō, Ueno Park
stops.narration:
Stand on the bluff above Shinobazu Pond and look at the building in front of you: a wooden hall on stilts, its covered stage jutting out over the slope as if about to step into the air. This is Kiyomizu Kannon-dō, built in 1631 and named, with typical Edo cheek, after Kyoto's far more famous Kiyomizu-dera — because a hall perched on a wooden stage above a drop is exactly what kiyomizu, clear water, describes. It is one of the oldest buildings standing in Ueno Park, and it sits on ground that was sacred long before there was a park at all.

This was Edo, and this hill was its holy quarter. In 1625 a monk named Tenkai, adviser to the early Tokugawa shōguns — the shōgun being the military ruler who governed while the emperor reigned as a figurehead in Kyoto — founded Kan'ei-ji here: a temple complex the size of a small town, dozens of halls spread across this plateau and down to the water. The site was chosen deliberately. In Buddhist cosmology the north-east is the demon gate, the direction from which evil approaches a ruler's castle, and Kan'ei-ji stood between Edo Castle and that danger.

On 4 July 1868 this hill became a battlefield. The shogunate had already fallen and imperial forces held Edo, but roughly two thousand loyalists calling themselves the Shōgitai barricaded themselves around Kan'ei-ji. The imperial army attacked from the high ground at Hongō with modern rifles and Armstrong cannons, and by late afternoon the position was taken and the temple was burning. It was never rebuilt. A monument nearby, put up by a later government at the request of the defenders' families, gives their numbers plainly — around 1,500 men against 10,000 — so you can see how the losing side is remembered here: not as traitors, but as soldiers loyal to a lost order.

The winner's memorial is the park itself. The new Meiji government confiscated the temple's land and in 1873 opened Ueno Park, among Japan's first public parks, laid out on the European model its officials had seen abroad. Then it filled the place with the hardware of a modern nation: the national museum traces back to Japan's first museum, opened in 1872, and art museums, a concert hall and a zoo followed. Walk the main avenue later and you pass them in a row.

The hall in front of you is older than all of that. Its main image is Senju Kannon, the thousand-armed Kannon, the Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion, and the custom here is specific: women come to pray for an easy childbirth and to leave small offerings for the child they hope for. Look to the left of the hall for the moon pine — a black pine with one long branch trained into a circle, an old trick for framing the full moon. It appears in Hiroshige's woodblock prints of Edo; the tree you see is a modern replacement of the same conceit. Entry is free, and the grounds and hall are usually open roughly 9am to 5pm, so verify at the gate. The museums, the fountain and the zoo are north of here on the park's main avenue — worth another visit. For now, leave by the path heading south-east out of the park, toward the railway. The market is just beyond it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter the hall and grounds. Donations are possible but never required.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 9:00 to 17:00, sometimes with seasonal variation. Verify at the gate; Ueno Park itself never closes.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free. The temple sits above a slope and the hall is reached by steps; the stage has a low rail and a drop below it. The park's main avenues are paved and level, and a wheelchair route to the bluff is available from the park side.
stops.insiderTip: Do not photograph only the hall — walk around to its left for the moon pine, the black pine with a branch trained into a ring. It is the detail in Hiroshige's prints and the one thing most visitors miss.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the temple by the path heading south-east out of the park toward the railway. In about five minutes you reach the road on the park's eastern edge; cross it and drop into the narrow street running under the elevated tracks. That is Ameyoko. If you have time first, the museums and the big fountain are a short detour north along the park's main avenue.

stops.name: Ameyoko Market
stops.narration:
You can hear this market before you see it: plastic crates, auction voices, a bell, somebody shouting the price of tuna. Ameyoko runs for roughly half a kilometre under and beside the railway tracks, from Ueno Station down toward Okachimachi, and it is the loudest survivor of a very specific moment — the years just after 1945, when Japan was hungry and the official economy did not work.

Understand what a black market was here. After the war, food was rationed and the ration was never enough, so the authorities tolerated an unofficial market where farmers from the surrounding countryside could sell directly to city people. This strip of land, alongside the Ueno rail yards, filled with improvised stalls selling vegetables, rice, fish, and — the profitable part — goods that had leaked out of American military bases. Several hundred stalls stood here at the peak. That is where the name comes from. Ameya can mean candy shop, because sugar was scarce and sweets turned up here first; it can also mean America, because surplus American goods did. Both stories are told, and both are probably half-right.

Today there are more than two hundred and fifty shops. The trade has shifted with the customers: cheap clothing and shoes, cosmetics and drugstore goods, then dried fish, seaweed, spices and fruit. Watch what Japanese shoppers are buying rather than what visitors photograph — the year-end rush here in the last days of December is famous across the country, when households come for the fish and the festival prices and the street becomes a crush.

Notice two things as you walk. First, the negotiation culture. Prices are often marked, but the theatre is not: shopkeepers call out, weigh, and shout the deal. This is the shitamachi, the old low city of merchants and artisans, and its commercial style is noisy, informal and personal. Second, look up now and then. The market grew along the railway embankment because the land beneath the tracks had no other use. Cheap land, cheap goods, high footfall — an economy in three moves.

Most shops open around 10am and shut around 8pm; many take a rotating Wednesday off, and individual hours vary, so treat the street as a morning-to-evening place and check as you go. It is free to walk — you only pay for what you eat or carry away. Eat something fried, then leave by the northern end and walk up into the quiet: from the top of the market, head north-west across Ueno's back streets, and the crowds fall away within two blocks.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. You pay only for what you buy; food is cheap and usually eaten standing up. Most shops take cash, though larger ones now take cards and IC transit cards.
stops.openingHours: Hours are per shop, not per street: most open around 10:00 and close around 20:00, with some restaurants later and many shops resting a rotating Wednesday. Weekends and the year-end period are by far the busiest.
stops.accessibility: Mostly flat, but the paving under the elevated tracks is uneven and patched, and the lane is narrow and often packed shoulder to shoulder. No steps on the main street; crossing the roads at either end needs care.
stops.insiderTip: Ignore the souvenir stands and watch what locals queue for — the fishmongers, the dried-fruit stalls and the spice shops. Prices at the year-end rush are famous, but the theatre of the shout is on display all year.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the northern end of the market, near Ueno Station, walk north-west out of the crowds and keep going through the quiet residential streets of Uenosakuragi and Yanaka. It is about two and a half kilometres, roughly thirty-five minutes on foot, and the character changes within two blocks. If you would rather ride, take the JR Yamanote line one stop from Ueno to Nippori and walk five minutes to the shopping street; the walk is the better half of this tour.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Maarten Heerlien from Voorschoten, The Netherlands, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yanaka Ginza
stops.narration:
This is a shotengai — a shopping street, and in Japan the word names an institution, not just a road. Yanaka Ginza is about a hundred and seventy metres long and three metres wide, with some sixty small shops, nearly all family-run and none of them a chain. The lane took its present shape in the decades after the war, and it has kept the proportions of that era: two-storey wooden fronts, canvas awnings, shopkeepers living above the shop, a butcher beside a tea seller beside a sweets shop that has sold the same thing for fifty years. In the boom years more than ten thousand people a day came here for tofu, fish and vegetables. Supermarkets took most of that trade in the 1990s, and across Japan thousands of streets like this one pulled down their shutters for good. This one did not, and the reason is partly stubbornness and partly address: it sits deep enough inside Yanaka that the big developers never quite bothered.

Walk it slowly and you can see what the neighbourhood did to survive. Shops turned family trades into things a passer-by wants — the butcher sells hot minced-meat cutlets, the tea shop sells single cups, the greengrocer sells fruit on a stick. The shopkeepers' association sets rules: no chain stores, new frontages must match the old ones, the street stays pedestrian. That is an argument about what a shopping street is for, and it is not the argument most of Tokyo had.

Then there are the cats. Yanaka has a real population of street cats, and they are not accidental: local people feed them and — the part that matters — neuter and manage them, so the colony stays small and healthy instead of growing. The neighbourhood has embraced them entirely. The street's mascot is a cat; there are cat-shaped doughnuts, cat ceramics, cat stationery; small wooden cats are hidden on the rooftops and awnings and finding them is a local game. The cats themselves sleep on the warm asphalt and on the steps and mostly ignore you. One honest note: they belong to the residents, not to visitors. Watch, photograph only if the cat agrees, and do not feed them.

Shops generally run from about 10am to 6pm, many close one weekday — often Monday or Tuesday — and the lane empties fast after dark, so do not save this for the evening. The food is cheap and mostly eaten standing: mince cutlets, croquettes, fish-shaped cakes, soft-serve. Buy something, then walk to the eastern end and climb the steps. They are the next stop, and they are best as the light goes.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Food and goods are at shop prices; most snacks cost a few hundred yen, and small stalls are cash-friendly, so carry coins.
stops.openingHours: Most shops roughly 10:00 to 18:00, with many taking one weekday off (often Monday or Tuesday). The street is always walkable, but it is a shopping street, not a night street — come before late afternoon.
stops.accessibility: The lane itself is flat and wide enough for a wheelchair, but it is only three metres across and can be shoulder-to-shoulder at weekends. The northern end is reached by the 36 steps of the Sunset Stairs; the step-free approach is from Sendagi, to the west, which is flat.
stops.insiderTip: Look up. Seven small wooden cat statues are hidden on the awnings and rooflines along the street — finding all of them is the local game. Then buy whatever the queue is queuing for; the lines usually know.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk east along the lane to its far end, where the street runs into a stone staircase rising to the bluff. Climb it — thirty-six steps — and you are on the Sunset Stairs, the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Yoshikazu TAKADA from Tokyo, Japan, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yuyake Dandan (Sunset Steps)
stops.narration:
Thirty-six steps, four metres of climb, and one of the best-known names in Tokyo. Yuyake is the glow of the setting sun; dandan is children's language for steps. Sunset Stairs. The name is young — it came from a public competition run in a local community newspaper around 1990, when the steps were rebuilt — but it stuck, because the view earns it. Turn around and face west.

Here is what you are looking at, and why it matters. The plateau behind you is the Nippori bluff, the northern edge of the same high ground that Ueno Park sits on. A step down and a hundred metres ahead, Yanaka Ginza lies flat below, its roofs and lanterns stacked up toward you, and beyond them the low city goes on and on toward the Sumida River and the bay. That height difference is not decoration; it is the reason this neighbourhood exists in its old form. The flatlands flooded and burned; the plateau was drier, cooler and, crucially, less likely to be consumed when fire swept the low city — which it did, again and again, until concrete and wars replaced wood.

The steps face almost due west, which is why the name works. In February the sun sets soon after five in the afternoon — a little after 5pm at the start of the month, nearer half past by the end — and the shopping street below turns copper for a few minutes. Arrive ten minutes early. On a clear winter evening the sky behind the rooftops goes pink, then violet, and the low roofs go dark.

You are also standing on a ward boundary. Behind you is Arakawa ward; the street below is Taitō ward. Nippori Station is three minutes to your right, which is why this is where the city arrives: commuters come off the Yamanote loop line and walk down these steps on the way home. That is the small, real pleasure of the view — it is not a platform built for tourists. It is how people get home, and it happens to be beautiful.

The steps are free and open at all hours. They are steps, though: thirty-six of them, no ramp, and the bypass slope to the left is steep. If you are avoiding stairs, come at the street from Sendagi instead, which is flat. When the light has gone, come back down part-way and head south-west through the lanes. The shrine with the red gates is about fifteen minutes away.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open at all hours. There is nothing to buy here except the view; the shops are back down on the street behind you.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The reason to come is the hour before sunset — roughly 4:45 to 5:30pm in February, later in summer.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: thirty-six steps with no ramp. A steep bypass slope runs to the left of the stairs. Wheelchair users and anyone with limited mobility should approach Yanaka Ginza from the flat Sendagi side instead and view the steps from the bottom.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the top rather than halfway down — the frame fills with the street's lanterns and rooflines. Then turn around and look the other way for a moment: the station platforms and the Keisei Skyliner are your onward route.
stops.nextStopDirections: Go back down the steps a few metres and turn south into the lanes rather than returning along the shopping street. Wind south-west through the residential blocks of Yanaka for just over a kilometre — about eighteen minutes, quiet, with temple walls on both sides — and you arrive at the big red torii gate of a shrine, which is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Emma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Nezu Shrine
stops.narration:
You are at the entrance to a Shinto shrine, so a few words first, because the terms matter and nobody is born knowing them. Shinto is Japan's indigenous religion of kami — spirits or sacred presences, in places, forces and ancestors rather than in a single god. A shrine is where a kami is honoured. The torii, the gate that looks like a tall doorway with a bar across the top, marks the boundary between ordinary ground and the shrine's ground: passing under it, you step out of the everyday.

This shrine is among the oldest places of worship in Tokyo, though almost nothing here is as old as the legend. Tradition dates its founding to the first century, nearby; what you can see was moved to this spot in 1705 by the fifth Tokugawa shōgun, Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, and built in 1706. The main hall, the worship hall and the offering hall are joined under one roof in a style called ishi-no-ma-zukuri, and the tower gate and the lattice-windowed wall around the sanctuary carry the same 1706 date. All of them are designated Important Cultural Properties — the second tier of national protection, below National Treasure. They have stood through the 1923 earthquake and the 1945 firebombing, which makes this one of the very few places in the city where you stand in front of intact early-eighteenth-century shrine architecture, in its original place, in a working parish.

The kami here is Susanoo-no-Mikoto, a storm-and-sea deity from Japan's oldest myths. Watch what people do and copy it. Bow slightly once as you pass the torii, and walk at the side of the path rather than down the middle — the centre is traditionally left clear for the kami. At the water basin near the entrance, take a ladle, pour water over your left hand, then your right, then a little into your left palm to rinse your mouth; that is purification, and it takes fifteen seconds. Do not photograph the inner sanctuary, and keep voices low. Entry is free and there is no obligation to pray or pay: a coin in the offering box is a courtesy, not a fee.

The reason most visitors come is the azalea garden on the slope to the left — roughly 6,600 square metres, some three thousand plants of about a hundred varieties, tended here for centuries. In late April and early May the whole hillside goes up in colour for the Bunkyō Azalea Festival, and the garden charges a small entry then; in recent years it has ranged from about ¥300 to ¥1,000 depending on how the bloom is doing, so check at the gate. In February the azaleas are bare stems and the garden is shut. Look anyway — the shape of the hillside is legible — and climb the path of vermilion torii on the hillside, past a small pond and a viewing platform, to the little Otome Inari shrine at the top. The tunnel of gates is as good as anything in Kyoto, with a fraction of the company.

The grounds are typically open from early morning to around 5pm, sometimes later in summer; verify locally. Then walk north-east, out of the shrine and into the residential lanes.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter the shrine precincts. The azalea garden charges only during the spring festival (roughly ¥300 to ¥1,000 in recent years, varying with the bloom). Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Precincts typically open daily from early morning to around 17:00, sometimes later in summer. The azalea garden opens only during the festival, roughly April to early May, about 9:30 to 17:30.
stops.accessibility: The main precinct is level gravel and stone. The hillside torii path climbs steps and is not step-free, and the azalea garden is on a slope with uneven paths. Benches near the main hall.
stops.insiderTip: The crowd photographs the main hall; the better move is the tunnel of vermilion torii up the hillside to Otome Inari, with the koi pond viewing platform halfway. Go before mid-morning for an empty path.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the shrine by its north side and walk north-east through the quiet residential lanes for about a kilometre and a half — twenty minutes or so, following the cemetery walls. The gates of Yanaka Cemetery open off the lane ahead; enter at the south end and walk the long central avenue north.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wiiii, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yanaka Cemetery
stops.narration:
Step through the gate and the city changes volume. This is Yanaka Cemetery: about ten hectares, roughly seven thousand graves, and a hundred and fifty years of Tokyo's dead — politicians, painters, novelists, doctors and a saint. It is free, it is open around the clock, and it is a working cemetery, not a sight. Walk and talk accordingly.

The place began as temple ground. Tennō-ji, a Buddhist temple, stood here from the seventeenth century, and the long straight road you are walking was its approach. Then in the 1870s the new Meiji government separated Buddhism from Shinto by decree — a policy meant to purify Shinto by cutting its centuries of entanglement with Buddhist institutions — and in doing so stripped temples of much of their land and their monopoly on funerals. The growing city needed public burial grounds, so this temple graveyard was declared a public cemetery for Tokyo, the largest in the country at the time. That is why the layout still feels like a temple's: long avenues, ranked stone graves, small shrines, and water taps for washing headstones.

The famous dead are here in numbers, and three of them make the point about what Japan chooses to honour. Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shōgun, who handed back power in 1867 and then lived quietly for another forty-five years, lies in a walled Tokugawa enclosure — look through the barred gates. Shibusawa Eiichi, the industrialist who helped build modern Japanese finance and business and involved himself in hundreds of companies and charities, is buried here too; since 2024 his face has been on the ¥10,000 note, Japan's most-used banknote. And Higuchi Ichiyō, a novelist who died of tuberculosis at twenty-four in 1896, having written sharp, unsentimental stories about women and poverty in the shitamachi, was on the ¥5,000 note from 2004 until the notes were redesigned in 2024. A shōgun, a banker and a novelist sharing the same few hectares: that is roughly the modern Japanese pantheon, and it is not arranged by rank.

Look for the ruin in the middle of the central avenue: the stone base of a five-storey pagoda that stood here from 1908 until a summer night in 1957, when it was destroyed in an arson that also killed two people who had planned to die there. It was never rebuilt. If you have time, walk the whole avenue — in April it is a tunnel of cherry blossom, which is why it is called Cherry-blossom Avenue, and in February the bare branches let you see the geometry of the graves.

Two practical notes. First, why a graveyard survives in the middle of a city: partly history, partly fire. Yanaka came through the 1923 earthquake and the firebombing of March 1945 in far better shape than the flatlands around it, and this huge open ground — cemetery, temple yards, wide lanes — is one of the reasons usually given. The exact mechanism is still argued over; the result is not. Second, etiquette. No picnics, low voices, no photographing mourners or funerals, and do not touch the flowers and water left on graves. This is somebody's family plot. That is the whole point. Leave by the north-west edge and walk into Sendagi, the last stretch of the walk.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public cemetery, open to all, with no ticket and no gate fee; the management office keeps daytime hours.
stops.openingHours: Effectively open at all hours and free, with no closing gate; the management office is staffed during the day. Come in daylight — it is a cemetery, and the light is better.
stops.accessibility: The central avenue and main paths are wide and gently graded gravel and stone, with no steps; some side paths toward the old pagoda site are narrower and uneven. Very little seating. The ground is a cemetery, with kerbs around grave plots.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Tokugawa enclosure gates and the flat stone base of the burned 1957 pagoda, both easy to walk past. And check whether the cherry avenue is in bloom — in April this is one of the finest hanami spots in the city and almost nobody outside the neighbourhood knows it.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk the central avenue north, then leave by the cemetery's north-west side and follow the lanes into Sendagi. It is just under a kilometre — about fifteen minutes — to the quiet streets around Sendagi Station, where the final stop is.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Guilhem Vellut from Annecy, France, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sendagi
stops.narration:
Sendagi is quiet, residential and easy to miss, which is exactly why it still works. The name is written with characters meaning a thousand bundles of wood, and the usual explanation is that firewood for the temples and the shōgun's kitchens was stockpiled here — a reminder that before gas and electricity this entire city was a machine for burning wood, and that its chronic, defining disaster was fire. Edo's proverb had it that fires and fights were the flowers of Edo, which tells you how routine both were.

The neighbourhood's other identity is literary. Mori Ōgai — novelist, translator, playwright, literary critic and, professionally, an army surgeon — lived from 1892 until his death in 1922 in a house on this street that he called Kanchōrō, the tide-watching tower, after the view from his second-floor study. Five minutes from the station, the Bunkyō City Mori Ōgai Memorial Museum now stands on the site, holding his manuscripts and belongings: it generally opens 10am to 6pm, closes the fourth Monday and Tuesday of each month, and charges admission that varies by exhibition, so check at the door. His neighbours in this quarter included a startling share of the writers who invented modern Japanese prose, and the reason is ordinary and human — it was cheap, it was on the edge of the city, and the lanes at night were quiet enough to write in.

What you have walked through today is the argument Tokyo keeps having with itself. The city's power and money sit on the western hills, in the yamanote: height, headquarters, glass. The old low city is where small trades still live, in two-storey buildings on three-metre lanes, and it survives here through a run of accidents — a plateau, a cemetery, a war that stopped short, and neighbours who organised in the 1980s to keep the towers off the skyline. None of that guarantees the next fifty years. You can already see new apartment blocks at the edges of the lanes, and the question of how much should change is being argued block by block.

End in the right place, though. You are standing among carpenters' workshops, small temples, a neighbourhood bathhouse or two and a shopping street that still sells dinner. That is not a museum of old Tokyo. It is Tokyo — someone's everyday, not a reconstruction of it.

When you leave: Sendagi Station, on the Chiyoda metro line, is two minutes away. Nezu Station is ten minutes south, and Nippori Station — the JR Yamanote loop and the Keisei Skyliner express to Narita Airport — is about fifteen minutes east, either back through the cemetery or along Yanaka Ginza and up the Sunset Steps. If you would rather eat first, head west into the lanes toward Nezu, where small restaurants open around six.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. The Mori Ōgai Memorial Museum charges an admission that varies by exhibition; verify at the door. Neighbourhood restaurants and the museum are cash- and card-friendly.
stops.openingHours: The lanes are open at all hours; this is a residential neighbourhood, so keep your voice down in the evening. The Mori Ōgai Memorial Museum generally runs 10:00 to 18:00 and closes the fourth Monday and Tuesday of each month.
stops.accessibility: Flat and step-free through the main lanes, with narrow pavements and a couple of kerb steps into shops. Sendagi Station has lift access to the Chiyoda line.
stops.insiderTip: You finish in the lanes about two minutes north of Sendagi Station, which is where this stop's pin sits. This is the quiet end of the walk and the best place to sit down: pick a café or a small restaurant here rather than heading straight for the train, and give the neighbourhood an hour — it is the closest you get to ordinary residential Tokyo on this route.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Sendagi Station on the Tokyo Metro Chiyoda line is two minutes away and connects to Otemachi and the centre; Nippori Station, about ten minutes east, has the JR Yamanote loop and the Keisei Skyliner to Narita Airport. Otherwise stay put: the lanes here are full of small places to eat, and the evening is theirs.
